Global Economy Set for Weakest Run Since 2008 Outside of Recessions

# Global Economy Set for Weakest Run Since 2008 Outside of Recessions

Heightened trade tensions and policy uncertainty are expected to drive global growth down this year to its slowest pace since 2008 outside of outright global recessions, according to the World Bank’s latest Global Economic Prospects report.

2025 Growth Forecasts Cut for 70 Percent of Economies

WASHINGTON, June 10, 2025—[tweetquote:[tweetText=Heightened trade tensions and policy uncertainty are expected to drive global growth down this year to its slowest pace since 2008 outside of outright global recessions,tweetData=WorldBank,tweetHash=GEP2025]], according to the World Bank’s latest Global Economic Prospects report. The turmoil has resulted in growth forecasts being cut in nearly 70% of all economies—across all regions and income groups.

[tweetquote:[tweetText=Global growth is projected to slow to 2.3 percent in 2025, nearly half a percentage point lower than the rate that had been expected at the start of the year. A global recession is not expected.,tweetData=WorldBank,tweetHash=GEP2025]] Nevertheless, if forecasts for the next two years materialize, average global growth in the first seven years of the 2020s will be the slowest of any decade since the 1960s.

“Outside of Asia, the developing world is becoming a development-free zone," said Indermit Gill, the World Bank Group’s Chief Economist and Senior Vice President for Development Economics. “It has been advertising itself for more than a decade. Growth in developing economies has ratcheted down for three decades—from 6 percent annually in the 2000s to 5 percent in the 2010s—to less than 4 percent in the 2020s. That tracks the trajectory of growth in global trade, which has fallen from an average of 5 percent in the 2000s to about 4.5 percent in the 2010s—to less than 3 percent in the 2020s. Investment growth has also slowed, but debt has climbed to record levels.”

[tweetquote:[tweetText=Growth is expected to slow in nearly 60 percent of all developing economies this year, averaging 3.8 percent in 2025 before edging up to an average of 3.9 percent over 2026 and 2027.,tweetData=WorldBank,tweetHash=GEP2025]] That is more than a percentage point lower than the average of the 2010s. Low-income countries are expected to grow 5.3 percent this year—a downgrade of 0.4 percentage point from the forecast at the start of 2025. Tariff increases and tight labor markets are also exerting upward pressure on global inflation, which, at a projected average of 2.9 percent in 2025, remains above pre-pandemic levels.

[tweetquote:[tweetText=Slowing growth will impede developing economies in their efforts to spur job creation, reduce extreme poverty, and close per capita income gaps with advanced economies. ,tweetData=WorldBank,tweetHash=GEP2025]][tweetquote:[tweetText=Per capita income growth in developing economies is projected to be 2.9 percent in 2025—1.1 percentage points below the average between 2000 and 2019.,tweetData=WorldBank,tweetHash=GEP2025]] Assuming developing economies other than China are able to sustain an overall GDP growth of 4 percent—the rate forecast for 2027—it would take them about two decades to return to their pre-pandemic trajectory with respect to economic output.

[tweetquote:[tweetText=Global growth could rebound faster than expected if major economies are able to mitigate trade tensions,tweetData=WorldBank,tweetHash=GEP2025]]—which would reduce overall policy uncertainty and financial volatility. The analysis finds that [tweetquote:[tweetText=if today’s trade disputes were resolved with agreements that halve tariffs relative to their levels in late May, global growth would be 0.2 percentage point stronger on average over the course of 2025 and 2026. ,tweetData=WorldBank,tweetHash=GEP2025]]

“Emerging-market and developing economies reaped the rewards of trade integration but now find themselves on the frontlines of a global trade conflict,” said M. Ayhan Kose, the World Bank’s Deputy Chief Economist and Director of the Prospects Group. “The smartest way to respond is to redouble efforts on integration with new partners, advance pro-growth reforms, and shore up fiscal resilience to weather the storm. With trade barriers rising and uncertainty mounting, renewed global dialogue and cooperation can chart a more stable and prosperous path forward.”

The report argues that [tweetquote:[tweetText=in the face of rising trade barriers, developing economies should seek to liberalize more broadly by pursuing strategic trade and investment partnerships with other economies and diversifying trade,tweetData=WorldBank,tweetHash=GEP2025]]—including through regional agreements. [tweetquote:[tweetText=Given limited government resources and rising development needs, policymakers should focus on mobilizing domestic revenues, prioritizing fiscal spending for the most vulnerable households, and strengthening fiscal frameworks. ,tweetData=WorldBank,tweetHash=GEP2025]]

[tweetquote:[tweetText=Finally, to accelerate economic growth, countries will need to improve business climates and promote productive employment by equipping workers with the necessary skills ,tweetData=WorldBank,tweetHash=GEP2025]]and creating the conditions for labor markets to efficiently match workers and firms. [tweetquote:[tweetText=Global collaboration will be crucial in supporting the most vulnerable developing economies, including through multilateral interventions, concessional financing,tweetData=WorldBank,tweetHash=GEP2025]] , and, for countries embroiled in active conflicts, emergency relief and support.

Regional Outlooks:

East Asia and Pacific: Growth is expected to slow to 4.5% in 2025 and to 4.0% in 2026–27. For more, see regional overview.

Europe and Central Asia: Growth is expected to slow to 2.4% in 2025 before edging up to 2.6% in 2026–27. For more, see regional overview.

Latin America and the Caribbean: Growth is projected to remain steady at 2.3% in 2025 before firming to an average of 2.5% in 2026–27. For more, see regional overview.

Middle East and North Africa: Growth is expected to rise to 2.7% in 2025 and further strengthen to an average of 3.9% in 2026–27. For more, see regional overview.

South Asia: Growth is projected to moderate to 5.8% in 2025 and firm to an average of 6.2% in 2026–27. For more, see regional overview.

Sub-Saharan Africa: Growth is expected to edge up to 3.7% in 2025 and average 4.2% in 2026–27. For more, see regional overview.
